entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 13 1Co 13:1-13 . Charity or Love Superior to All Gifts. The New Testament psalm of love, as the forty-fifth Psalm (see Psa 45:1 , title) and the Song of Solomon in the Old Testament. 1. tongues-- from these he ascends to "prophecy" ( 1Co 13:2 ); then, to "faith"; then to benevolent and self-sacrificing deeds: a climax. He does not except even himself, and so passes from addressing them ("unto you," 1Co 12:31 ) to putting the case in his own person, "Though I," &c. speak with the tongues-- with the eloquence which was so much admired at Corinth (for example, Apollos, Ac 18:24 ; compare 1Co 1:12 ; 3:21 , 22 ), and with the command of various languages, which some at Corinth abused to purposes of mere ostentation ( 1Co 14:2 , &c.). of angels-- higher than men, and therefore, it is to be supposed, speaking a more exalted language. charity-- the principle of the ordinary and more important gifts of the Spirit, as contrasted with the extraordinary gifts ( 1Co 12:1-31 ). sounding ... tinkling-- sound without soul or feeling: such are "tongues" without charity. cymbal-- Two kinds are noticed ( Psa 150:5 ), the loud or clear, and the high-sounding one: hand cymbals and finger cymbals, or castanets. The sound is sharp and piercing.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17036"/><div sID="gen33716" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17036"/><hi type="bold">2. mysteries--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.11.25">Ro 11:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25">16:25</reference>). Mysteries refer to the deep counsels of God hitherto secret, but now revealed to His saints. Knowledge, to truths long known.<div eID="gen33716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faith ... remove mountains--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.17.20">Mt 17:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.21">21:21</reference>). The practical power of the will elevated by faith [Neander]; confidence in God that the miraculous result will surely follow the exercise of the will at the secret impulse of His Spirit. Without "love" prophecy, knowledge, and faith, are not what they seem (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.1">1Co 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.2">2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.7.22">Mt 7:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.14">Jas 2:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.8">1Co 13:8</reference>), and so fail of the heavenly reward (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.2">Mt 6:2</reference>). Thus Paul, who teaches justification by faith only (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.4">Ro 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.16">Ga 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7-2Cor.3.14">3:7-14</reference>), is shown to agree with James, who teaches (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.24">Jas 2:24</reference>) "by works" (that is, by LOVE, which is the "spirit" of faith, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.26">Jas 2:26</reference>) a man is justified, "and not by faith only." <div eID="gen33717" type="x-p"/>

Knowledge, to truths long known. faith ... remove mountains-- ( Mt 17:20 ; 21:21 ). The practical power of the will elevated by faith [Neander]; confidence in God that the miraculous result will surely follow the exercise of the will at the secret impulse of His Spirit. Without "love" prophecy, knowledge, and faith, are not what they seem (compare 1Co 8:1 , 2 ; Mt 7:22 ; Jas 2:14 ; compare 1Co 13:8 ), and so fail of the heavenly reward ( Mt 6:2 ). Thus Paul, who teaches justification by faith only ( Ro 3:4 , 5 ; Ga 2:16 ; 3:7-14 ), is shown to agree with James, who teaches ( Jas 2:24 ) "by works" (that is, by LOVE, which is the "spirit" of faith, Jas 2:26 ) a man is justified, "and not by faith only."

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17037"/><div sID="gen33718" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17037"/><hi type="bold">3. bestow ... goods ... poor--</hi>literally, "dole out in food" all my goods; one of the highest functions of the "helps" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.28">1Co 12:28</reference>).<div eID="gen33718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">give ... body to be burned--</hi>literally, "to such a degree as that I should be burned." As the three youths did (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.28">Da 3:28</reference>), "yielded their bodies" (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.15">2Co 12:15</reference>). These are most noble exemplifications of love in giving and in suffering. Yet they may be without love; in which case the "goods" and "body" are given, but not the soul, which is the sphere of love. Without the soul God rejects all else, and so rejects the man, who is therefore "profited" nothing (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.26">Mt 16:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.23-Luke.9.25">Lu 9:23-25</reference>). Men will fight for Christianity, and die for Christianity, but not live in its spirit, which is love. <div eID="gen33719" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17039"/><div sID="gen33725" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17039"/><hi type="bold">5. not ... unseemly--</hi>is not uncourteous, or inattentive to civility and propriety.<div eID="gen33725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thinketh no evil--</hi>imputeth not evil [Alford]; literally, "the evil" which actually is there (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.12">Pr 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.8">1Pe 4:8</reference>). Love makes allowances for the falls of others, and is ready to put on them a charitable construction. Love, so far from devising evil against another, excuses "the evil" which another inflicts on her [Estius]; doth not meditate upon evil inflicted by another [Bengel]; and in doubtful cases, takes the more charitable view [Grotius]. <div eID="gen33726" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17040"/><div sID="gen33727" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17040"/><hi type="bold">6. rejoiceth in the truth--</hi>rather, "rejoiceth with the truth." Exults not at the perpetration of iniquity (unrighteousness) by others (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.9.22">Ge 9:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.9.23">23</reference>), but rejoices when the truth rejoices; sympathizes with it in its triumphs (2Jo 4). See the opposite (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.8">2Ti 3:8</reference>), "Resist the truth." So "the truth" and "unrighteousness" are contrasted (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.8">Ro 2:8</reference>). "The truth" is the Gospel truth, the inseparable ally of love (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.15">Ep 4:15</reference>; 2Jo 12). The false charity which compromises "the truth" by glossing over "iniquity" or unrighteousness is thus tacitly condemned (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.15">Pr 17:15</reference>). <div eID="gen33727" type="x-p"/>

See the opposite ( 2Ti 3:8 ), "Resist the truth." So "the truth" and "unrighteousness" are contrasted ( Ro 2:8 ). "The truth" is the Gospel truth, the inseparable ally of love ( Ep 4:15 ; 2Jo 12). The false charity which compromises "the truth" by glossing over "iniquity" or unrighteousness is thus tacitly condemned ( Pr 17:15 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17042"/><div sID="gen33732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17042"/><hi type="bold">8. never faileth--</hi>never is to be out of use; it always holds its place.<div eID="gen33732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall fail ... vanish away--</hi>The same Greek verb is used for both; and that different from the Greek verb for "faileth." Translate, "Shall be done away with," that is, shall be dispensed with at the Lord's coming, being superseded by their more perfect heavenly analogues; for instance, knowledge by intuition. Of "tongues," which are still more temporary, the verb is "shall cease." A primary fulfilment of Paul's statement took place when the Church attained its maturity; then "tongues" entirely "ceased," and "prophesyings" and "knowledge," so far as they were supernatural gifts of the Spirit, were superseded as no longer required when the ordinary preaching of the word, and the Scriptures of the New Testament collected together, had become established institutions. <div eID="gen33733" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17047"/><div sID="gen33748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17047"/><hi type="bold">13. And now--</hi>Translate, "But now." "In this present state" [Henderson]. Or, "now" does not express time, but opposition, as in <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.11">1Co 5:11</reference>, "the case being so" [Grotius]; whereas it is the case that the three gifts, "prophecy," "tongues," and "knowledge" (cited as specimens of the whole class of gifts) "fail" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.8">1Co 13:8</reference>), there abide permanently only these three--faith, hope, charity. In one sense faith and hope shall be done away, faith being superseded by sight, and hope by actual fruition (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.24">Ro 8:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.7">2Co 5:7</reference>); and charity, or love, alone never faileth (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.8">1Co 13:8</reference>). But in another sense, "faith and hope," as well as "charity," ABIDE; namely, after the extraordinary gifts have ceased; for those three are necessary and sufficient for salvation at all times, whereas the extraordinary gifts are not at all so; compare the use of "abide," <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.14">1Co 3:14</reference>. Charity, or love, is connected specially with the Holy Spirit, who is the bond of the loving union between the brethren (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.30">Ro 15:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.8">Col 1:8</reference>). Faith is towards God. Hope is in behalf of ourselves. Charity is love to God creating in us love towards our neighbor. In an unbeliever there is more or less of the three opposites--unbelief, despair, hatred. Even hereafter faith in the sense of trust in God "abideth"; also "hope," in relation to ever new joys in prospect, and at the anticipation of ever increasing blessedness, sure never to be disappointed. But love alone in every sense "abideth"; it is therefore "the greatest" of the three, as also because it presupposes "faith," which without "love" and its consequent "works" is dead (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.6">Ga 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.17">Jas 2:17</reference>, 20).<div eID="gen33748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but--</hi>rather, "and"; as there is not so strong opposition between charity and the other two, faith and hope, which like it also "abide." <chapter eID="1Cor.13"/>
